conversation.content: We've been designing a Twitter-like feed system. Let's go deep on content moderation. Start with the first line of defense — automated detection. How do you detect problematic content before it reaches users?

Automated detection operates in multiple layers, each optimized for different content types and threat categories. For images and videos: the first check is perceptual hash matching against known databases of illegal content, like PhotoDNA for CSAM (Child Sexual Abuse Material) and the GIFCT shared hash database for terrorism content. PhotoDNA generates a robust hash that survives resizing, cropping, and color adjustments. We compute the hash at upload time and compare against the database — this is a legal obligation in many jurisdictions and the match threshold is tuned for near-zero false negatives even at the cost of some false positives. For novel image content (not in any hash database), we run ML classifiers: an NSFW classifier (trained on labeled datasets, typically a fine-tuned ResNet or EfficientNet), a violence/gore classifier, and a hate symbol detector. Each produces a confidence score from 0 to 1. For text content: we run a toxicity classifier — something like Google's Perspective API or a custom BERT-based model fine-tuned on our platform's labeled data. The model classifies text into categories: toxic, severe toxic, identity attack, insult, threat, sexually explicit. We also run regex-based and keyword-based filters for known slurs and spam patterns as a fast pre-filter before the ML model. For links: check against URL reputation databases (Google Safe Browsing, PhishTank) for phishing and malware URLs. All these checks run in a moderation pipeline that processes content asynchronously — the tweet is published immediately but enters a 'pending review' state internally. If any classifier flags the content above its threshold, the tweet is held from the feed until reviewed.
You mentioned ML classification for text toxicity. How do you train and maintain these models?

Training a toxicity classifier is an ongoing process, not a one-time effort. Initial training data: we start with public datasets like the Jigsaw Toxic Comment dataset (~160K labeled comments) and augment with platform-specific labeled data. The platform-specific data is critical because toxicity is context-dependent — terms that are slurs in general English might be reclaimed terms used positively in certain communities on our platform. The model architecture: a fine-tuned transformer (DistilBERT for latency-sensitive inference, or a larger BERT variant for batch processing). Input: the tweet text, tokenized. Output: multi-label probabilities for each toxicity category. Training: standard fine-tuning with cross-entropy loss, with class weighting to handle the severe class imbalance (toxic content is ~2-5% of all content). Active learning loop: the model's most uncertain predictions (confidence between 0.4-0.6) are routed to human reviewers. Their labels become new training data. This focuses human effort on the boundary cases that most improve the model. We retrain monthly with the accumulated new labels. Model evaluation: we maintain a 'golden set' of ~5000 hand-labeled examples that never enters training. Every model version is evaluated against this set. Key metrics: precision (to control false positives — removing legitimate speech is harmful), recall (to catch violating content), and per-category F1 scores. We require precision > 0.85 and recall > 0.90 before deploying a new model version. Adversarial robustness: users actively try to evade classifiers with leetspeak (h4te), homoglyphs (using Cyrillic 'а' instead of Latin 'a'), and Unicode tricks. We add a text normalization step before classification that canonicalizes these evasion attempts, and we regularly evaluate the model against an adversarial test set.
Automated systems will make mistakes. How does the human review queue work?

The human review queue receives content from three sources: automated classifier flags (medium-confidence detections), user reports (other users flagging content as violating), and appeals (users contesting an automated removal). The queue is prioritized: CSAM and terrorism content are always P0 (review within 1 hour — this is a legal requirement under EU DSA), content flagged by multiple users is P1 (review within 4 hours), single-user reports and medium-confidence classifier flags are P2 (review within 24 hours). Reviewers (trust and safety analysts) see the content, its context (the thread, the author's history, the reporter's history), and the classifier's confidence scores and category labels. They choose an action: approve (content is fine), remove (violates policy), restrict (reduce distribution but don't remove — used for borderline content), or escalate (needs legal review or policy team input). Quality assurance: 10% of decisions are randomly audited by senior reviewers. Reviewers are evaluated on accuracy (agreement with auditor), speed, and consistency with other reviewers (inter-rater reliability). If a reviewer's accuracy drops below 90%, they receive additional training. Reviewer well-being: moderating toxic content takes a psychological toll. We implement mandatory breaks every 2 hours, limit shifts to 6 hours per day on graphic content queues, provide access to mental health resources, and blur graphic imagery by default (reviewer clicks to reveal). These aren't just ethical obligations — burned-out reviewers make worse decisions.
What about the appeals process? A user says their content was wrongly removed.

Appeals are essential for fairness and are legally required in many jurisdictions (EU DSA mandates an appeals mechanism). The process: the user receives a notification explaining what was removed and which policy it violated (transparency). They can submit an appeal with an explanation of why they believe the decision was wrong. The appeal goes into a separate review queue — critically, it's reviewed by a different reviewer than the one who made the original decision, to avoid confirmation bias. The appeal reviewer sees: the original content, the original reviewer's decision and reasoning, the user's appeal text, and additional context (the user's overall account standing, the original reporter's history of reports — are they a serial false-reporter?). Possible outcomes: upheld (removal stands), overturned (content is restored, and the reporter may receive a notification that their report was unfounded), or policy exception (content technically violates the letter of the policy but is clearly newsworthy, satirical, or educational — these are the hardest calls). If the user is still unsatisfied, EU DSA provides for an out-of-platform dispute resolution mechanism, which we need to support. Metrics I'd track on appeals: appeal rate (what percentage of removals are appealed — high rates suggest over-moderation), overturn rate (what percentage of appeals are overturned — high rates confirm over-moderation), and time to resolution (target: 72 hours). These metrics feed back into model and policy improvements — if a specific toxicity category has a 30% overturn rate on appeal, the classifier threshold for that category needs adjustment.
How do you handle false positives — legitimate content that gets incorrectly flagged or removed?

False positives are arguably more damaging to the platform than false negatives in the long run, because they erode user trust and chill legitimate speech. Detection of systemic false positives: I'd monitor removal rates by content category, user demographic, language, and topic. If removals spike for a particular language (say Arabic) or topic (say political protest discussion), that's a signal the classifier may be biased or a new policy is being over-applied. A/B testing with held-out groups: randomly exempt 1% of flagged content from automated removal, let human reviewers evaluate it, and measure the false positive rate. If 20% of auto-removed content would have been approved by a human, the classifier threshold is too aggressive. Per-user impact tracking: if a user has 3+ pieces of content removed in a week but has an otherwise clean 2-year history, their most recent removal should be auto-escalated for human review — it's likely a false positive cluster. Recovery from false positives: when content is restored (via appeal or proactive review), we restore its original position in the feed timeline rather than re-inserting it at the current time. We notify the author that the content has been restored with an apology. If the content was viral before removal, we also consider boosting its distribution to compensate for the interruption. At the systemic level, each false positive is a labeled data point — we add it to the training set as a negative example. Quarterly, we audit the most common false positive patterns and adjust either the model or the policy.
Strong deep dive on content moderation. You covered the technical ML aspects and the human and legal dimensions. Thank you.

strengths: Comprehensive moderation pipeline from automated hash matching through ML classification to human review
Strong attention to regulatory requirements (EU DSA, CSAM reporting obligations)
Thoughtful false positive handling with multiple detection and recovery mechanisms
weaknesses: Did not discuss the infrastructure architecture — how the moderation pipeline scales to handle millions of posts per day
No capacity estimation for the moderation queue or the ML inference infrastructure
